title: Shakshuka with Feta
subtitle: eggs poached in spiced tomato sauce with feta
excerpt: Eggs poached directly in a thick, spiced tomato and pepper sauce, finished with crumbled feta. It is bold, warming, and needs only one pan. Eat straight from the pan with crusty bread.
sourceNotes: Shakshuka is eaten across North Africa, the Middle East, and Israel. Its exact origin is debated -- Tunisia, Libya, and Yemen all have strong claims. It became iconic in Israel through North African Jewish immigrants.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the tomato sauce ahead and refrigerate. Add eggs and feta when reheating.

content.text: Use a wide pan so the eggs have room to cook without touching each other. Keep the heat low when the eggs go in. Runny yolks need only 6 to 8 minutes. Cover the pan with a lid to trap steam and cook the tops.
Heat olive oil in a wide frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion for 5 minutes until soft.
Add the red pepper and cook for another 5 minutes.
Add the garlic, cumin, smoked paprika, and chilli flakes. Cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the tinned tomatoes. Stir and simmer for 10 minutes until the sauce is thick. Season with salt.
Scatter half the feta over the sauce.
Make 6 wells in the sauce with a spoon. Crack one egg into each well.
Cover the pan with a lid. Cook over low heat for 6 to 8 minutes until the whites are set but the yolks are still runny.
Scatter the remaining feta over the top and serve directly from the pan.

items.cause: Heat too low or pan not covered
items.fix: Cover the pan with a lid. The steam is what cooks the tops of the whites. A higher heat for the last 2 minutes also helps.
Check after 6 minutes. The yolks should still wobble when the pan is moved.

items.cause: Not reduced enough before adding eggs
items.fix: Simmer the sauce for 5 more minutes until it is thick. A watery sauce spreads the eggs out and they take longer to cook.

content.text: Shakshuka is claimed by multiple countries across North Africa and the Middle East. Tunisia, Libya, and Israel all have strong connections to the dish. It became widely popular in Israel through the large Sephardic and North African Jewish communities who brought it with them from the Maghreb. Today it is eaten at any time of day and appears on restaurant menus across the world.
